hints: Focus on what is common to every neutralisation reaction, no matter which acid or alkali you use.
Think about what happens with a diprotic acid like $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: one mole of acid makes two moles of water, so the heat released is doubled.
To keep the value fair and comparable, the definition must fix the amount of the one product made in all cases.
walkthrough:
**Recall what neutralisation really is**

Think of it simply as hydrogen ions meeting hydroxide ions to make water. That is the heart of every acid-alkali reaction.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{H}^{+}(aq) + \text{OH}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

**See why per mole of acid or alkali does not work**

Different acids and alkalis make different amounts of water. For example, one mole of $\text{HCl}$ makes one mole of water, but one mole of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ makes two moles of water and releases about twice the heat.

**Fix the definition on water**

To make it standard, we define it per mole of water formed under standard conditions from aqueous acid and aqueous alkali. That gives the same $\Delta H^{\ominus}_{neut}$ of about $-57 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for all strong acid, strong alkali reactions.

options.A: This is wrong because one mole of acid does not always make one mole of water. A diprotic acid like $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ makes two moles, so this definition would give double the true value.
options.B: This is wrong for the same reason as A, but from the alkali side. Some alkalis provide two moles of $\text{OH}^{-}$ per mole, so one mole of alkali can make more than one mole of water.
options.C: This is a tempting trap because it sounds balanced and neat. However, one mole reacting with one mole still does not guarantee one mole of water if the acid or base is dibasic, so it is not the standard definition.
options.D: This is correct. Standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is the enthalpy change when an aqueous acid and aqueous alkali react to form one mole of water under standard conditions. This works for all acids and alkalis.
